correspondence.finding: The chosen opening is an unnamed foothill draw entering the cultivated eastern intermontane lowland. The southward/eastward hook and subsequent northward turn lie in the same broad piedmont and lowland setting. No distinct river name or precisely surveyed source is established.

The northward selection follows the eastern cultivated lowland, with pale alluvial surfaces and diffuse channel-like traces between the mountain flanks. Its westward bend remains within this same broad receiving depression and piedmont corridor. Scattered field boundaries and local drainage traces are not assigned independent names or current hydraulic functions.

The long northwestward and then westward selection crosses cultivated plain and piedmont surfaces toward the head of the western collector. The municipal relief map shows separate short drainage traces rather than this whole connecting course; the original imagery shows agricultural plots and diffuse local runoff patterns but does not establish a continuous selected transfer between the eastern depression and the western collector. This is an intervening connection gap, distinct from the accepted terminal-playa continuation.

Below the northwestern bend, a visible southward collector and its low corridor lead into the elongated pale playa. Municipal drainage linework supports the western collector and adjacent tributary setting. The broad entry and receiving setting are established; no precise or currently wetted channel is asserted.

The remaining southward and southeastward continuation, including the final bend and actual selected ending, stays within one continuous elongated playa/lowland. The original western image covers its northern entry, broad central floor, southeastern extension and endpoint setting. A river trace across the playa floor is neither required for this bounded correspondence nor claimed. The waterbody or lowland has no selected-feature name established by the material read.

The municipal map/table identify Río Bajío San Agustín on a transverse eastern tributary entering the western lowland. That label is not demonstrated to name the selected northern approach or the whole system. Río San Pablo, Presa El Carmen and Laguna de Labradores are separately depicted regional features, not established aliases or selected lake/reservoir passages. No separately supplied tributary fragment, glacier connection or demonstrated managed-channel passage is present.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen unnamed feeder southeast of Lone Grave Butte
correspondence.finding: The chosen opening follows a mapped intermittent ravine on the southeastern side of Lone Grave Butte, then bends southwest and west toward the northern Guano Valley wetland. The unnamed feeder and the successive lower bends are depicted; no name is inferred from Lone Grave Butte or nearby roads.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern Guano Valley wetland and slough entry
correspondence.finding: The feeder enters the northern Guano Valley marsh/depression setting and the selected northward continuation enters the mapped Guano Slough corridor. The receiving setting and its northern exit are covered at ordinary scale; a presently wetted channel is not required. Guano Lake and Shirk Lake farther south are not traversed by this chosen opening.

correspondence.component_scope: Guano Slough canyon and northeastern turn
correspondence.finding: Repeated Guano Slough labels follow the selected northward canyon, the eastward turn, Black Canyon and the approach to Guano Reservoir. The intervening stored joins remain within the same mapped valley corridor. Alger Lake, Link Lake and Murphy Waterhole are neighboring features rather than substitute selected reaches.

correspondence.component_scope: Guano Reservoir and lower slough bend
correspondence.finding: The mapped slough enters Guano Reservoir at the canyon mouth and continues northeast into a multithread intermittent slough. The selected broad northward bend is generalized west of the depicted principal thread and rejoins its lower branches. At ordinary corridor scale the connected reservoir and lower-slough setting is covered; no exact reservoir-bank, outlet-vertex or individual-thread claim is made.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Guano Slough and Rock Creek Sinks approach
correspondence.finding: Lower Guano Slough divides into intermittent channels and reaches the wetland/sink belt labeled Rock Creek Sinks. The selected northeastern approach and its entry into that receiving setting are depicted; channel diffusion in the sinks is not itself a gap.

correspondence.component_scope: Rock Creek Sinks to eastern Catlow wetland transfer
correspondence.finding: The selected continuation turns east from Rock Creek Sinks and then southeast across the central Catlow plain toward the eastern wetland. Topography shows intervening low contour ridges, small ponds, separated intermittent drainage traces and the Blitzen Valley Road crossing. The independently read imagery shows the western sink belt and eastern wetland separated by differently textured plain/ridge and pond areas, but no complete selected geographic through-link. The observation does not assert a hydraulic barrier; the connection remains unestablished. Shared ancient Lake Catlow or modern basin membership is insufficient, and this is not simply the lack of one wetted thread on a continuously depicted receiving fan.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern Catlow wetland and Garrison Lake approach
correspondence.finding: The selected route continues south through the broad eastern Catlow marsh-and-pond corridor, passing west of mapped West Field Lake. Marshes, intermittent collectors and the northern Garrison Lake entry are depicted. Home Creek is a separate eastern tributary; neither it nor West Field Lake is assigned to the selected mainstem as a whole.
The selected route enters the northern Garrison Lake wetland and crosses the mapped lake/playa body toward its southern margin. Garrison Lake is an intervening lake, not the actual selected endpoint.

correspondence.component_scope: Continuation south of Garrison Lake and actual ending
correspondence.finding: South of Garrison Lake, the original imagery shows the selected continuation remaining within an elongated, continuous low-lying lakebed/marsh-and-pond receiving setting through to the actual endpoint. Topography places Stockwater Ditch nearby and across part of the vicinity, but the selected ending lies west of the mapped ditch rather than on its depicted southern end. The terminal receiving setting is geographically accounted for without requiring a blue line across its dry floor or a currently wetted thread. No name is assigned to the ending or to small unlabeled ponds; Garrison Lake remains an intervening lake.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern highland opening and southward feeder
correspondence.finding: The original regional map depicts the chosen eastern opening southwest of the San Pedro Calacollo area, its southwest-to-south continuation beside the Uyo label and Anquipiña, and the successive eastern Catani/Aruma-side tributary mouths. All four selected parts remain in that mapped receiving valley. The smaller H1 Figure3.4 labels the upper feeder Q. Luyo. The two spellings are retained as source-specific reach references, not declared registry aliases.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Upper feeder in the Luyo/Uyo–Anquipiña setting; no precise name transition assigned

correspondence.component_scope: Upper westward turn and Challaviento-side junction
correspondence.finding: The map follows the westward valley from the Catani/Aruma-side junction past the Caplina and Chachacoman locality setting to the northwestern Challaviento-side drainage. This is the selected long westward part and its actual receiving junction. The source does not make the unselected northwestern headwater the chosen source merely because its river label is clearer.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Selected headward branch joining the Caplina receiving valley

correspondence.component_scope: Chachacoman to Challatita middle valley and tributary joins
correspondence.finding: The continuous mapped valley runs southwest below Chachacoman, through the Pulaca/Focaña-side mouths and the Palca receiving junction toward Challatita. All five part boundaries occur on this same valley. H1 authorial prose identifies Palca as a main Caplina tributary; Palca is kept as a tributary name rather than applied to the selected upstream branch.

The blue mapped channel continues past the Tocucó/Calientes junction and through the Pachía, San José and Calana cultivated valley. Regional field observations name the Caplina at Velasquez–Calana. The selected joins and intervening parts remain on the depicted receiving corridor.

The selected southward continuation beside Calana and Piedra Blanca follows the mapped diversion-side channel toward the eastern Tacna drainage. GA-45A printed31 explicitly identifies the Piedra Blanca river as Uchusuma and a diversion of Caplina; its printed35 photo caption independently identifies the Caplina diversion. The nearby Represa Cerro Blanco is east of the selected route and is not assigned as a through-reservoir crossing. Imagery corroborates the cultivated valley and managed eastern-city connection at ordinary corridor scale, without resolving present routing among individual control structures.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Caplina diversion toward the Uchusuma corridor

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern Tacna to Gregorio Albarracín and the Arunta continuation
correspondence.finding: The selected southwestward passage follows the mapped channel along eastern and southern Tacna and Gregorio Albarracín, then the Arunta receiving corridor. The regional map and H1 network distinguish neighboring Cobani/Viñani branches and depict their receiving joins. The connected route is supported without treating all these reach names as interchangeable. Imagery corroborates the valley alongside the built-up area and its southward opening into the lower wash.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Connected Uchusuma/Arunta receiving reach of the representative Caplina system

correspondence.component_scope: Arunta–Hospicio alluvial fan and Los Palos approach
correspondence.finding: The mapped lower channel continues through the Arunta–La Garita junction setting and southwest as Hospicio, beside Las Lagunas toward Los Palos. Both original maps depict this continuous alluvial receiving corridor. PET describes loss of surface flow in the desert, while H1 explains that the coastal channel is usually dry because of irrigation, infiltration and evaporation. These statements limit flow claims rather than remove the mapped geographic continuation. The imagery independently shows the receiving dry-wash/fan corridor through the agricultural plain and its gradual spread into the terminal cultivated fan.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Arunta and Quebrada Hospicio lower receiving corridor

correspondence.component_scope: San Pedro y San Pablo coastal terminal
correspondence.finding: The final selected part meets the coast near San Pedro y San Pablo, northwest of Las Palmeras and Conchal. The regional original depicts the channel to this coastal receiving setting; H1 depicts the Hospicio continuation to the Pacific separately from the adjacent Las Salinas and Escritos outlets. This establishes ordinary terminal correspondence, not a perennial open mouth or exact present shoreline. The imagery shows the same continuously covered lower fan entering the coast. Agricultural subdivision and diffuse distributaries do not create a missing cross-basin transfer.
correspondence.named_reach_scope: Hospicio fan outlet in the Los Palos Pacific-coast setting

correspondence.finding: The selected opening lies in the eastern low valley among partly snow-covered elongated waterbodies. The original image shows its short northern indentation, western turn, and southwest continuation through the same connected low-waterbody/stream corridor. Snow obscures small shoreline details, but the ordinary valley and waterbody connection remains readable; no alternative basin crossing is required. No individual lake or feeder name is assigned.

The eastern original follows the westward waterbody/stream sequence into the larger irregular dark-water widening and its southwest outlet. The intervening joins remain in one continuous valley. Seasonal snow and the imagery seam change appearance, not the geographic through-connection. Lake and outlet names are not supplied by the imagery.

Overlapping eastern and middle originals show the southwest outflow turning through broad meanders, then north and west into the same river valley. The widening, bends and intermediate joins correspond at corridor scale; the selected generalized line is not interpreted as an exact present bank.

The middle original shows the westward reach turning southwest into the incised corridor, continuing across the central bends and pale gravelly reaches. Adjacent tributary valleys join this same collector without a selected divide crossing or unresolved waterbody passage. All selected intermediate joins are covered.

Overlapping middle and western originals show the western canyon continuation, the lower bend northward, and the broader gravelly river valley leading to the coastal plain. These selected parts remain within the same continuous river corridor; nearby lakes and tributaries are not promoted to the representative name.

The western original follows the lower valley into the broad fan-shaped delta, including the northern delta-side continuation and adjacent spit/lagoon shore, and out to its open-bay receiving setting. ARC403 independently identifies this coastal fan delta as the Brock River entering the southeastern corner of Darnley Bay and distinguishes the neighboring Hornaday delta. The selected terminal is a generalized delta-to-bay continuation; no precise distributary, wetted thread across the spit, shoreline vertex, or navigation condition is asserted.
